title: Short Stuff: Obituaries
summary: Short Stuff episode on obituaries. The hosts discuss the rise of obituary websites and genealogy research using obituaries, and note that early obituaries were mostly for famous people. They cover the mid-nineteenth-century shift to short "death notices," how hand-set type limited newspaper length until the Linotype arrived in the 1880s, and how newspapers began charging by the line, which made obituaries a moneymaker. They describe the classic four-part obituary format that took shape in the 1930s and 1940s, the practical and legal side (death certificates are required but publishing an obituary is not, and funeral homes typically handle submission), and how obituaries became more personal and honest after September 11, 2001. They close with a story about adult children who wrote that their mother would not be missed, which drew public backlash.

segments.title: Opening banter and obituary readership
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode on obituaries, joke about who reads them, and mention the Beyond the Dash website and the genealogy value of obituaries.

segments.title: Early obituaries and famous people
segments.summary: Hosts say early obituaries were mostly for famous people. They mention pre-written obituaries at major papers and note the shift to short death notices in the mid-nineteenth century.

segments.title: Hand-set type and the Linotype
segments.summary: Obituaries were brief because newspapers were set by hand until the Linotype came along around the 1880s, which made larger papers easier to produce.

segments.title: Civil War, Victorian death culture, and obituaries as revenue
segments.summary: Civil War deaths increased death notices, and Victorian fascination with death added to this. Newspapers began charging people to list loved ones in obituary columns, which turned them into a moneymaker. Statistics show obituary counts and their share of newspaper pages grew from 1900 to the 1930s.

segments.title: Classic obituary format and the pre-written obit
segments.summary: The classic four-part obituary format took shape in the 1930s and 1940s. The hosts joke about writing their own obituaries.

segments.title: Legal side, cost, and who writes the obituary
segments.summary: A death certificate is legally required, but publishing an obituary is not. Funeral homes typically submit obituaries, the family provides the content and pays, often by the line.

segments.title: Post-September 11 honesty and the unmissed mother
segments.summary: After September 11, 2001, obituaries became more personal and honest, including about causes of death like suicide. The hosts then discuss a case where adult children wrote that their mother would not be missed, which caused public backlash.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts wrap up the episode and sign off.
